From Old Norse félagi (“companion”), derived from fællig, Old Norse félag (“fellowship”), a compound of fé (“wealth”) + lag (“place, fellowship”). The English word fellow is borrowed from Old Norse.
Originally genitive of fællig, Old Norse félag (“fellowship”), a compound of fé (“wealth”) + lag (“place, fellowship”).

parole.significato: community (only in the prepositional phrase i fællig).
parole.testo: From Old Norse félag (“fellowship”), a compound of fé (“wealth”) + lag (“place, fellowship”).
From Old Danish færth, from Old Norse ferð, from Proto-Germanic *fardiz. Cognate with German Fahrt (“journey, speed”). Doublet of fart (“speed”)).
From Old Norse ferðask, derived from ferð (< færd), from Proto-Germanic *fardiz.
From Old Danish færthigh, from Old Norse ferðugr. Partly influenced by Middle Low German verdich. Compare German fertig.
From Old Norse ferja, from Proto-Germanic *farjǭ, cognate with Swedish färja, English ferry, German Fähre. Derived from the verb *farjaną, see below.

parole.significato: to ferry, transport something by ferry
parole.testo: From Old Norse ferja, from Proto-Germanic *farjaną, cognate with Swedish färja, English ferry, Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐍂𐌾𐌰𐌽 (farjan, “to sail”). Related to the verb *faraną (“to go, travel”).

parole.significato: Faroese, Faroe Islander (a person from the Faroe Islands)
parole.testo: From Old Norse færeyingr. See also Irish fearann.
From Old Danish fæstæ, from Old Norse festa, from Proto-Germanic *fastijaną, cognate with Norwegian feste, Swedish fästa, German festen. Derived from *fastuz (“firm”).

From Old Danish føthæ, from Old Norse fœða f, from Proto-Germanic *fōdijǭ, which is only found in North Germanic. Related words are *fōdīniz (in Middle Low German vōde, Middle High German vüete, Gothic 𐍆𐍉𐌳𐌴𐌹𐌽𐍃 (fōdeins)) and *fōdô (in English food).
From Old Danish føthæ, from Old Norse fœða, from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną, cognate with Swedish föda, English feed, Dutch voeden.
From Old Norse fyl (“foal”), from Proto-Germanic *fulją. English foal and German Fohlen go back to a different derivation from the same root, Proto-Germanic *fulô (whence Old Norse foli).
From Old Danish fylghæ, from Old Norse fylgja, from Proto-Germanic *fulgijaną (“to follow”), related to Proto-Germanic *fulgāną in English follow and German folgen.
From Old Norse fylgi. Derived from the verb.

From Old Norse fyrr, from Proto-Germanic *furi, *furiz (“for, before”). Cognates include Swedish före, för, English for, and German für. A different form of the same word, Proto-Germanic *furai, is found in Danish for and German vor.
From Old Danish før, from Old Norse fœrr, from Proto-Germanic *fōriz (“able to go”), a verbal adjective of Proto-Germanic *faraną (“to go”) Danish fare.
From Old Norse fœri, derived from the adjective Old Norse fœrr (Danish før).
From Old Norse fœra, from Proto-Germanic *fōrijaną, cognate with Swedish föra, German führen, Dutch voeren. A causative from *faraną (“to go”) (Danish fare).
From føre (“to lead”) + -ing, from Old Norse fœring, partly influenced by Middle Low German voringe.
From Old Norse fyrstr, from Proto-Germanic *furistaz, cognate with Swedish först, English first, German Fürst (“prince”, noun). Doublet of fyrste.
From Old Norse gap, verbal noun to gapa (“to gape”).
From Old Norse gapa

parole.significato: street (a paved part of road, usually in a village or a town)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gatæ, from Old Norse gata, whence English gate. Cognate with German Gasse (“lane”), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍄𐍅𐍉 (gatwō).
From Old Danish galæn, from Old Norse galinn (“enchanted, mad”), a past participle of gala (“to sing, chant”) (Danish gale (“to crow”)).
From Old Norse gal (“shouting”), derived from the verb gala (“to sing, chant”) (Danish gale (“to crow”)).
From Old Danish gallæ, from Old Norse gall, from Proto-Germanic *gallǭ.

parole.significato: sorcery, wizardry, spell, incantation (particularly in Old Norse times)
parole.testo: From Old Norse galdr, from Proto-Germanic *galdraz.

parole.significato: to crow (mostly of the sound of the cock)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gala (“to sing, crow, chant”), from Proto-Germanic *galaną, cognate with Norwegian gale, Swedish gala, English gale.

parole.significato: gallows (wooden framework on which persons are put to death by hanging)
parole.testo: From Old Danish galghæ, from Old Norse galgi, from Proto-Germanic *galgô, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰalgʰ-, *ǵʰalg- (“long switch, rod, shaft, pole, perch”).
From Old Norse galti, galtr, gǫltr, from Proto-Germanic *galtuz.

parole.significato: a vulture or condor; scavenging birds living in Africa, Europe, Asia and America
parole.testo: From Old Danish gam, from Old Norse gammr, gambr. Cognate with Old High German gampilun, gabilun (“a fablelike creature”).

parole.significato: old (having existed for a relatively long period of time)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gamæl, from Old Norse gamall (“old”), from Proto-Germanic *gamalaz, cognate with Swedish gammal, Dutch gammel. The comparative and the superlative are formed from a different stem: ældre, ældst, from Old Norse ellri, ellztr, from Proto-Germanic *alþizô, *alþistaz, cognate with Englis
From Old Danish gamen, from Old Norse gaman, from Proto-Germanic *gamaną.

parole.significato: the act of walking, a walk
parole.testo: From Old Danish gang, from Old Norse gangr, from Proto-Germanic *gangaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ- (“stride, step”).
From Old Danish gangæræ, from Old Norse gangari (spelt also as gangvari).

parole.significato: to flirt with another person in a cheeky or sexual manner
parole.testo: Origin unknown. Possibly from the mediopassive Old Norse gantask (“to fool around”). Cognate with Icelandic gantast.
From Old Norse garn, from Proto-Germanic *garną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰorn-, *ǵʰer- (“gut, intestine”).
From Old Norse gassi.
From Old Norse gat, from Proto-Germanic *gatą.
From Old Norse gafl.
From Old Norse gjafmildr, influenced by gave (“gift”).

From Old Norse gagn, from Proto-Germanic *gagną, related with the preposition Proto-Germanic *gagin (“against”) in Danish gen- (“re-”), igen (“again”), gennem (“through”). The English noun gain is a loan from Old Norse.

parole.significato: to be of gain to, to benefit
parole.testo: From Old Norse gagna. Derived from the noun Old Norse gagn (“benefit”) (Danish gavn).
From Old Danish get, from Old Norse geit, from Proto-Germanic *gaits, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰayd- (“goat”). Cognates include Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍄𐍃 (gaits) and Latin haedus.
From Old Norse gedda.
From Old Danish gømæ, from Old Norse geyma, from Proto-Germanic *gaumijaną, cognate with Swedish gömma, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌿𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (gaumjan).
From the Old Norse preposition gegn; compare with igen (“again”) and Norwegian Bokmål gjen-.

parole.significato: to herd, shepherd, guide, impel (people or animals)
parole.testo: From Old Danish genæ, from Old Norse gegna, from Proto-Germanic *gaginjaną. Compare Old English gegegnian, German begegnen and Icelandic gegna.

parole.significato: through (in space, from one side to the other)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gegnum, dative of the adjective gegn (“right, fitting”), derived from the preposition gegn (“against”), from Proto-Germanic *gagin (“towards”). Compare also Danish igen, English again, against, German gegen, entgegen.
From the Old Norse preposition gegnum. See also gennem.

parole.significato: event or process characterized by adversity and difficulties.
parole.testo: From genvordig + -hed, from Old Norse gagnverðuligr.
From Old Norse geirr, from Proto-Germanic *gaizaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰays- (“pointed stick, spear”).
From Old Norse gjarna, gerna.
Verbal noun to gøre (“do, perform, execute”), from Old Norse gerning, gørning, gjǫrning.

From Old Danish getæ, gitæ (“to be able”), from Old Norse geta (“to get, guess”), from Proto-Germanic *getaną (“to acquire”). The Germanic verb is related to Latin prehendō (“to seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“take, seize”).
Old Norse gísl, from Proto-Norse ᚨᛊᚢᚷᛁᛊᚨᛚᚨᛊ (asugisalas), from *ᚷᛁᛊᛚᚨᛉ (*gislaʀ), from Proto-Germanic *gīslaz.
From Old Danish gift, from Old Norse gipt. Largely replaced by gave, from Middle Low German gave. The word still exists in some compound words, e.g. afgift.
From Old Norse gipta (“give away in marriage”), a specialized use of gipt (“gift”).
From Old Norse giptarmál.
From Old Norse gildi.
From Old Danish geldæ, from Old Norse gelda (“to castrate”), from Proto-Germanic *galdijaną.
From Middle Danish gelding, from Old Norse geldingr.

parole.significato: a gimmer, a ewe between one and two years old (hasn't had offspring yet)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gimmer, from Old Norse gymbr, from Proto-Germanic *gimrį̄. Cognate with Ancient Greek χίμαιρα (khímaira).

From Old Danish getse, gitse, getsa (“to guess”), from Old Norse *getsa, *gitsa, from Proto-Germanic *gitisōną (“to guess”), from Proto-Germanic *getaną (“to get”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to take, seize”). Cognate with Danish gåde (“a riddle”), Swedish gissa (“to guess”), Saterland Frisia
From Old Danish gespæ, gespæn. From Old Norse geispa.
Inherited from Old Danish gifæ, from Old Norse gefa, from Proto-Germanic *gebaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-.

Expected form is gælde, now obsolete. The current form originates likely from a Funen dialectal gjalde, gjalle. From Old Danish gællæ, *giallæ, from Old Norse gella, gjalla, from Proto-Germanic *gellaną (“to shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shout”).
From Old Norse gjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *gerdō. The Old Norse word has been borrowed into English girth.
From Old Danish glath, from Old Norse glaðr, from Proto-Germanic *gladaz
Old Norse glama

Compound of glar + mester. First word is from Old Danish glar, glaar, from Old Norse glar, Derived from Proto-Germanic *glasą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰel- (“to shine, glimmer, glow”). Cognates include Icelandic gler and Faroese gler. Doublet of glas.
Inherited from Old Norse glas(keri), itself borrowed from Middle Low German glas, from Old Saxon glas.
From Old Danish glømæ, from Old Norse gleyma. Compare Swedish glömma, Faroese gloyma and Norwegian Nynorsk gløyma.

From Old Danish glænte, from a verb originally meaning "glide," from Old Norse *glenta, *gletta, from Proto-Germanic *glentaną (“to slide; glide”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰlend- (“to shine; sparkle; look”).
From Old Norse glóa (“to glow”), from Proto-Germanic *glōaną.
From Old Norse gleypa (“to devour”).

parole.significato: a peephole, opening, window (in the ceiling, wall etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gluggr. Related to glo.
From Old Danish glæthæ, from Old Norse gleði.
From Old Danish glæthæ, from Old Norse gleðja, from Proto-Germanic *gladjaną.
From Old Norse glóð. See also glo.
From Old Norse glœða. See glød.
From Old Norse gnaga. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål gnage, Norwegian Nynorsk gnaga, Swedish gnaga, German nagen, Dutch knagen. Probably from Proto-Indo-European *gʰnēgʰ- (“to gnaw, scratch”).
From Old Norse gneisti, from Proto-Germanic *gahnaistô (“spark”), from *ga- + *hnaistô (“spark”), perhaps from the ultimate source of German knistern (“to crackle”).
From Old Norse gnubba.
From Old Norse gnyr.

parole.significato: to laugh or cackle, especially in a mischievous or malevolent way
parole.testo: From Old Danish gnægjæ, from Old Norse gneggja, from Proto-Germanic *hnajjaną. Cognates include Swedish gnägga, Icelandic hneggja, Faroese gneggja and Norwegian knegge.
Inherited from Old Danish gōþær, gothær, from Old Norse góðr (“good”), from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz. Cognate with English good and German gut.
From Old Norse góði m, from the adjective góðr (“good”). Compare, with a different suffix, German Güte.

parole.significato: godi (a priest in pre-Christian Scandinavia and in Nordic Neopaganism)
parole.testo: From Old Norse goði, from Proto-Germanic *gudô, a variant of *gudjô, which is the source of Proto-Norse ᚷᚢᛞᛁᛃᚨ (gudija) and Gothic 𐌲𐌿𐌳𐌾𐌰 (gudja, “priest”). Both words are derived from the noun *gudą (“god”) (Danish gud).
From Old Danish gotz, from Old Norse góz, a partitive genitive of góðr (“good”). Compare also Norwegian gods, Swedish gods.

Probably from or related to Old Norse geldr (“barren, yielding no milk”), from Proto-Germanic *galdaz, *galdijaz (“barren, unfruitful”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shout, cry”). See also Swedish gall (“barren”), German galt, gelt (“yielding no milk, unfruitful”), Old Norse gelda (“to castr
From Old Norse gramr, cognate with Icelandic gramur (“resentful, irritated”).
From Old Norse grǫn, from Proto-Germanic *granō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰroH-néh₂-.
From Old Danish grannæ, from Old Norse granni, from Proto-Germanic *garaznô (“neighbour”).

From Old Norse grǫf, gröf, from Proto-Germanic *grabą, *grabō (“grave, trench, ditch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrābʰ- (“to dig, scratch, scrape”). Compare Norwegian and Swedish grav, Icelandic gröf, English grave, West Frisian grêf, Low German Graf, Graff, Dutch graf, German Grab.

parole.significato: dig (to move hard-packed earth out of the way)
parole.testo: From Old Norse grafa (“to dig, bury”), from Proto-Germanic *grabaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrābʰ- (“to dig, scratch, scrape”).
From Old Norse grip. Related to gribe.
From Old Norse greip.

parole.significato: a branch, bough (protrusion of wood from the trunk of a tree)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gren, from Old Norse grein (“branch”), from Proto-Germanic *grainō. Maybe related to the verb *grīnaną, if the original meaning was "to yawn". The noun has replaced the older Germanic word for "branch", *astaz.

From Old Danish gryp, from Old Norse gripr (“vulture, griffin”) and Middle Low German grip, via Latin gryps, Derived from Ancient Greek γρύψ (grúps). Doublet of grif and kerub. Compare Old Irish gríb (“gyrfalcon, griffin”).

From Old Danish gripæ, from Old Norse grípa (“to grab”), from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb- (“to grasp, grab”). Cognate with Swedish gripa, Norwegian Bokmål gripe, Icelandic grípa, English gripe, West Frisian gripe, Low German griepen, Dutch grijpen, German greifen.
From Old Danish grim (“cruel, grim”), from Old Norse grimmr, from Proto-Germanic *grimmaz.
From Old Norse gríma f, from Proto-Germanic *grimô m (“mask; visor”). Cognates include English grime and grimace.
From Old Norse grína, from Proto-Germanic *grīnaną.

parole.significato: pig (a mammal of the family Suidae)
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse gríss.
Likely an amalgamation of Old Danish gresk from Old Norse gríð (“intenseness”). And Middle High German grit. Cognate with grådig (“greedy”)
From Old Norse gróa, from Proto-Germanic *grōaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreH₁-. Related to græs and grøn.
From Old Norse grunnr (“shallow”).
A convergence of two Old Norse words, grund (“a plain”) and grunn (“a shallow”).
From Old Norse grýjandi.
From Old Danish grytæ, from Old Norse grýta. Cognates include Swedish gryta, Norwegian Bokmål gryte.
From Old Danish gryn, from Old Norse grjón (“grain”).
From Old Norse *grynta, from Proto-Germanic *grunnōną (“to grunt”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrun- (“to shout”). Cognate with German grunzen (“to grunt”), English grunt.
From Old Norse grár, from Proto-Germanic *grēwaz.
From Old Norse grátr, from Proto-Germanic *grētaz. Cognate with Norwegian gråt, Swedish gråt, and Gothic 𐌲𐍂𐌴𐍄𐍃 (grēts). Derived from the verb Proto-Germanic *grētaną (“to weep”).
From Old Norse gráðugr, from Proto-Germanic *grēdagaz, cognate with English greedy, Dutch graag (“gladly”). Derived from the noun *grēduz (“desire”).
From Old Norse gráhærðr, from grár (“grey”) + hár (“hair”). Cognate with Norwegian gråhærd.

From Old Norse gráta (“cry”), from Proto-Germanic *grētaną, cognate with Norwegian gråte, Swedish gråta, and Gothic 𐌲𐍂𐌴𐍄𐌰𐌽 (grētan). From Frankish *grātan, the verb was borrowed to French regretter (whence English regret). The Danish form has generalized the vocalism of the preterit (cf. Old Norse g
From Old Danish græs, from Old Norse gras (“grass”), from Proto-Germanic *grasą.
From Old Danish grøt, from Old Norse grautr, From Proto-Germanic *grautiz, *grautaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewd-.
From Old Danish grøthæ, from Old Norse gróði. Related to gro.
From Old Danish gryft, from Old Norse grǫftr.
From Old Danish, from Old Norse grœnn, from Proto-Germanic *grōniz (“green”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreH₁- (“grow, become green”).

parole.significato: Greenlandic (of, from, or pertaining to Greenland, its people or language)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse grœnlenzkr, from Grœnland (“Greenland”).
From Old Norse guð (“god”), from Proto-Germanic *gudą. Cognate with English god and German Gott.

parole.significato: deity (a powerful entity that possesses numerous miraculous powers), divinity (deity)
parole.testo: From gud (“god”) + -dom (“-hood”), from Old Norse guðdómr.
From Old Danish guul, from Old Norse gulr, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”).

From Old Danish *guld, from Old Norse *gulð, *gulþ (compare Old Swedish guldh), variant of Old Norse gull, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”). Cognate to gul (“yellow”). Compare Runic Old East Norse: ᚴᚢᛚ (kul /⁠ḡull⁠/), ᛁᚢᛚ (iul /⁠jull⁠/).
From Old Danish gulz smith, from Old Norse gullsmiðr (“goldsmith”).
From Old Norse golf (“floor”), from Proto-Germanic *gulbą.
From Old Danish gomæn, from Old Norse gómr, gómi, from Proto-Germanic *gōmô. Compare Swedish gom.
From Old Norse gustr, cognate with English gust.

parole.significato: unnaturally or morbidly pale and yellowish in person, facial colour, or body part.
parole.testo: From Old Norse gustr. An archaic noun is gust, with the same meaning as in English, see gust.
From Old Danish giutæ, from Old Norse gjóta, from Proto-Germanic *geutaną, cognate with German gießen, Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (giutan), Latin fundō, Ancient Greek χεῖν (kheîn).
From Old Norse gyðja, from Proto-Germanic *gudjǭ.
From Old Norse gullinn (“golden”), from gull (“gold”).

parole.significato: A young sow that is pregnant for the first time.
parole.testo: From Old Norse gyltr.

From older gunge, from an unattested Old Danish *gunga, from Old Norse *gunga (found in the Old Norse proper noun Gungnir). Ablaut of Old Norse ganga, Danish gange, gænge, to the same root as going. Cognate to Swedish gunga.

parole.significato: to shiver, shudder (due to fear, cold etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gjósa, from Proto-Germanic *geusaną.
From Old Norse *gāʀ (East) / gær (West), from Proto-Germanic *gēz (“yesterday”).

parole.significato: farm, estate, land (property in the countryside)
parole.testo: From Old Danish garth, from Old Norse garðr, from Proto-Germanic *gardaz. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål gård, Swedish gård, English yard, Dutch gaard. Related to gærde (“fence, wall”).

From Old Danish gas, from Old Norse gás, from Proto-Germanic *gans, cognate with Swedish gås, English goose, German Gans, Dutch gans. The Germanic noun derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns (“goose”), which is also the source of Latin ānser, Ancient Greek χήν (khḗn), Lithuanian žąsi̇̀s, Sanskrit
From Old Danish giald, from Old Norse gjald n (“payment”), from Proto-Germanic *geldą, cognate with Swedish gäld c (archaic), English yield, German Geld n (“money”).
From Old Danish gialdæ, from Old Norse gjalda, from Proto-Germanic *geldaną (“to pay, have value”), cognate with Swedish gälda, English yield, German gelten.

From Old Norse gjǫlnar f pl, from Proto-Germanic *gelunō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel-, cognate with Norwegian gjelle, Swedish gäl (English gill is from Old Norse), and distantly related to Ancient Greek χεῖλος (kheîlos, “snout, beak, lip”).

parole.significato: yeast (froth used in medicine, baking and brewing)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gerð (“yeast”). Influenced by Middle Low German gere (“yeast”).

parole.significato: a fence or low wall (such as to demarcate a field or a garden)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gærthæ, from Old Norse gerði, derived from garðr (“enclosure, stronghold, wall”), whence gård (“yard, farm”)

parole.significato: only used in være i gære
parole.testo: From Old Norse gerð (“action, deed”).
From Old Norse gestr, from Proto-Germanic *gastiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“stranger, guest”).
From Old Danish giæf, gæf, from Old Norse gæfr (“comfortable”), from Proto-Germanic *gēbiz, cognate with Dutch gaaf (“complete, smooth”). Derived from the verb *gebaną (“to give”).

parole.significato: feed (a portion of food for domestic animals)
parole.testo: From Old Danish giæf, from Old Norse gjǫf (“gift”), from Proto-Germanic *gebō, cognate with Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌰 (giba). Derived from *gebaną (“to give”). A related word has replaced this word in its central meaning "gift", namely gave, which is probably a loan from Middle Low German gābe, from Proto-Germani
From Old Norse geyja (“bark”).
From Old Norse gœða, related to góðr (“good”).
From Old Danish gøræ, from Old Norse gera, gøra, gørva, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną. Cognate with Swedish göra, German gerben (“to tan”). Doublet of garve and gære.
From Old Danish hath, from Old Norse hatr, from Proto-Germanic *hataz, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂d- (“hate”).
From Old Norse hata, from Proto-Germanic *hatāną.
From Old Norse haka.
From Old Norse haki, from Proto-Germanic *hakô.
From Old Norse hǫkull, from Proto-Germanic *hakulaz, cognate with Norwegian Bokmål hagel (from Danish), Norwegian Nynorsk hakel, Swedish hake, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌺𐌿𐌻𐍃 (hakuls).
From Old Danish haghæl, from Old Norse hagl, from Proto-Germanic *haglą (“hail”), cognate with Norwegian hagl, Swedish hagel, English hail, German Hagel, Dutch hagel.
Old Norse hǫll (“large living room”)
From Old Norse hali.
From late Old Norse hala, from Middle Low German halen, from Old Saxon halon (“to get, fetch”).
From Old Norse halmr, from Proto-Germanic *halmaz.
From Old Norse hals, from Proto-Germanic *halsaz.
From Old Norse haltr
From Old Danish half, from Old Norse halfr (“half”), from Proto-Germanic *halbaz.
Equivalent to halv (“halv”) + anden (“other”), from Old Norse halfr annarr, compare Old English ōþer healf, German anderthalb.
Equivalent to halv (“half”) + femte (“fifth”), from Old Norse halfr fimmti, compare Old English fīfte healf, German fünfthalb (archaic).
Equivalent to halv (“half”) + fjerde (“fourth”), from Old Norse halfr fjórði, compare Old English feorþe healf, German vierthalb (archaic).
From Old Norse hamr, from Proto-Germanic *hamaz, *hamô.
Older hannem, from Old Norse hǫnum, the dative of hann (“he”). Compare Swedish honom.
From Old Norse hamarr, from Proto-Germanic *hamaraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱmoros, from *h₂éḱmō (“stone”).
From Old Norse hampr (“hemp”), from Proto-Germanic *hanapiz.
From Old Norse hann (dative hánum).
From Old Norse handla, hǫndla, from hǫnd (“hand”). In the sense trade influenced by from Middle Low German handelen and German handeln.
Old Norse handsal, see hånd and salg.

From Old Danish hanzkæ, from Old Norse hanzki, from Middle Low German hantsche, colloquial form of hantscho (“glove, gauntlet”), from Old Saxon handsko (“gauntlet, glove”) from hand (“hand”) and skōh (“shoe”) << Proto-West Germanic *skōh.
From Old Danish hanæ, from Old Norse hani, from Proto-Germanic *hanô, from Proto-Indo-European *kan- (“to sing”).
From Old Norse hari, heri (“hare”).
From Old Norse harka
From Old Danish harm, from Old Norse harmr, from Proto-Germanic *harmaz.
A variant to Old Danish harm (“anger, affront”), from Old Norse harmr.
From Old Danish harm (“anger, affront”), from Old Norse harma.
From Old Danish harpæ, from Old Norse harpa (“harp”), from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ. Compare Norwegian Bokmål harpe, Swedish and Icelandic harpa, German Harfe, Dutch and English harp.

From Old Norse harskr, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kars- (“to scratch, scrape, rub, card”). See also Middle Low German harsch (“hairy”), Russian короста (korosta, “to itch”), Old Church Slavonic краста (krasta).
From Old Norse harfr, herfi (“harrow”). Related to Ancient Greek καρπός (karpós), and Latin carpere.

parole.significato: hazel (tree or shrub of the genus Corylus)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hesli.
From Old Norse hattr, hǫttr.

parole.significato: sea; ocean (large body of salt water)
parole.testo: From Old Danish haf, from Old Norse haf, from Proto-Germanic *habą, cognate with Swedish hav, German Haff (“bay”) (from Low German).
From Old Danish haghi, from Old Norse hagi, from Proto-Germanic *hagô. Cognate with Norwegian hage, Swedish hage, English haw, German Hag, Dutch haag.

From Old Danish hauæ, from Old Norse hafa (“to have, wear, carry”), from Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to have, hold”), cognate with English have, German haben. The Germanic words are from Proto-Indo-European *kap- and are not related to Latin habeō.
From Old Norse hǫfn (“haven”), from Proto-Germanic *habnō, from Proto-Indo-European *kopno-.

From Old Danish hafræ, from Old Norse hafri, from Proto-Germanic *habrô, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish havre, English haver (dialect), German Hafer (from Low German), Dutch haver. Derived from the noun *hafraz (“he-goat”).
Compound of hav + torn, Old Danish haghthorn, from Old Norse hagþorn. Compare English hawthorn.
From Old Danish het, from Old Norse heitr.

parole.significato: to be called (to have a specific name)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hetæ, from Old Norse heita, from Proto-Germanic *haitaną (“to call”), cognate with Swedish heta, German heißen, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (haitan, “to call”).
From Old Norse heiðr (“heath, moor”).
From Old Norse hiti, hita.

parole.significato: (used with op / up) to heat, warm.
parole.testo: From Old Norse heita. Cognate with Old High German heizen.
From Old Danish hæthæn, from Old Norse héðan. Related to hen and hin.
From late Old Norse heiðneskr, after Middle Low German heidensch. Equivalent to heden (“heathen (archaic)”) + -sk.
From Old Danish hethen + -ing, from Old Norse heiðinn.

parole.significato: heron (long-legged, long-necked wading bird of the family Ardeidae)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hegri (“heron”).

parole.significato: whole, entire, complete, full (undivided, with all elements)
parole.testo: From Old Norse heill, from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, sound”), cognate with English whole, German heil, Dutch heel, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐌻𐍃 (hails).

Nominalisation of an old archaic adjective from Old Danish helbregde (“who is in good health”). From Old Norse heilbrigði. First part is from hel. Last part is related to Old Norse bragð (“moment, deed, advice”) and Old Norse bregða, see Danish bebrejde.
From Old Norse heill (“omen, happiness”), from Proto-Germanic *hailzą, from the adjective *hailaz (“whole, sound”) (Danish hel). Compare Norwegian hell.
From Old Danish hælgh, hælagh, from Old Norse helgr f, from Proto-Germanic *hailagijō, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish helg. Derived from *hailagaz (“holy”).
Old Norse heldr
Originally the neuter of an adjective corresponding to Old Norse heldri (“bigger”), see heldr (“rather”).
From Old Norse heilagr, from Proto-Germanic *hailagaz.

From Old Danish hælsæn, helse, from Old Norse heilsa, from Proto-Germanic *hailisǭ, cognate with Swedish hälsa. Ultimately derived from the noun *hailaz (“whole, sound”). Doublet of helse (“health”) and hilsen (“greeting”).

From Old Danish hælwitæ, from Old Norse helvíti, from Hel, hel (“the goddess of the realm of the dead”) (itself from Proto-Germanic *haljō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide, conceal”)) + víti (“punishment”). Compare Norwegian and Swedish helvete, Icelandic and Faroese helví
From Old Norse heimiligr, from Middle Low German heimelik, from Old Saxon *hēmlīk, from Proto-West Germanic *haimalīk.
From Old Norse henna, the dative of hón (“she”).
From Old Danish hæntæ, hæmtæ, from Old Norse heimta, from Proto-Germanic *haimatjaną.
From Old Norse hér.
From Old Norse herbergi.

From Old Norse hestr (“stallion”), from Proto-Germanic *hanhistaz, a Verner alternation variant of *hangistaz, which is the source of the West Germanic word for “stallion”, cf. German Hengst and Danish hingst (a loanword from Low German).

parole.significato: hither, to here, towards this place
parole.testo: From Old Danish hidh, from Old Norse hit.

From Old Danish helse, from Old Norse heilsa, from Proto-Germanic *hailisōną (“to salute, beseech”), cognate with Swedish hälsa (“to greet”), English halse (“to salute”), Old High German heilisōn (“to predict”).

From Old Danish himæn, himæl, from Old Norse himinn, from Proto-Germanic *himinaz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish himmel, English heaven, German Himmel. The modern Scandinavian form with -l is influenced by German.
From Old Danish himæriki, from Old Norse himiríki, himinríki, from himinn (“heaven”) + ríki (“kingdom”). Calque of Ancient Greek βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν (basileía tôn ouranôn).

From Old Danish hin, from Old Norse hinn. The other Germanic languages have a similar, but phonologically distinct pronoun in the same function: Proto-Germanic *jainaz, cf. Old English ġeon, Old High German jēner, and Gothic 𐌾𐌰𐌹𐌽𐍃 (jains).
From Old Norse hind, from Proto-Germanic *hindiz.
From Old Danish hinnæ, from Old Norse hinna, from Proto-Germanic *hinnǭ, cognate with Swedish hinna.
From Old Norse hinna (“to reach”), from Proto-Germanic *hinþaną, cognate with Swedish hinna (“to have sufficient time”), Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌷𐌹𐌽𐌸𐌰𐌽 (frahinþan, “to take captive”).
From Old Norse hindra, from Proto-Germanic *hinderōną, cognate with English hinder, German hindern. Derived from the adverb and preposition *hinder (“behind”).

parole.significato: bodyguard for a chieftain or king
parole.testo: From Old Norse hirð, from Old English hīred, from Proto-West Germanic *hīwarād.

parole.significato: there, thither (somewhere else than at the immediate spot)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hizi + at.
From Old Danish hittæ, from Old Norse hitta, from Proto-Germanic *hittijaną, cognate with Norwegian hitte, Swedish hitta, English hit (probably from Old Norse).
From Old Norse hjallr (“scaffold”), from Proto-Germanic *helþaz (“stack, frame”), cognate with Norwegian hjell, Swedish hjälle.
From Old Danish hælm, from Old Norse hjalmr (“helmet”), from Proto-Germanic *helmaz.
From Old Danish hēm, hiem, from Old Norse heimr, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz, cognate with Swedish hem, English home, German Heim, Ancient Greek κώμη (kṓmē).
From Old Danish hēm, hiem, from Old Norse heim, an adverbial accusative of the noun heimr, see above. Compare the adverbs Swedish hem, English home, German heim.

parole.significato: at home, home (in the place where one belongs, in a static position)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hemæ, hemmæ, from Old Norse heima (“at home”), an adverb from the noun heimr. Compare Swedish hemma, English at home, German daheim.
From Old Danish hemæl, from Old Norse heimild, heimuld.

From Old Danish hiarnæ, hiærnæ, from Old Norse hjarni (“brain”), from Proto-Germanic *hersô (“brain”), genitive *herznaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂s- (“head”). The same Germanic word is the source of Danish isse (“crown of head”), from Old Norse hjarsi, hjassi. A collective formation from this
From Old Danish hiærtæ, hiartæ, from Old Norse hjarta, from Proto-Germanic *hertô, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr (“heart”).
Inherited from Old Danish hion, hiona, from Old Norse hjón, from Proto-Germanic *hīwōnō.
From Old Danish hiorth, from Old Norse hjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *herdō, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish hjord, English herd, German Herde.
From Old Danish hiort, from Old Norse hjǫrtr, from Proto-Germanic *herutaz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish hjort, English hart, German Hirsch.

From Old Norse hjól, hvél, from Proto-Germanic *hwehwlą, cognate with Norwegian hjul, Swedish hjul, and English wheel. The Germanic noun originates from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlóm, *kʷékʷlos (“wheel”), which is also the source of Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos) (cf. cyclus) and Sanskrit चक्र (cakrá
From Old Danish hiælp, hialp, from Old Norse hjalp, derived from the verb hjalpa (“to help”), see hjælpe.
From Old Danish hiælpæ, hialpæ, from Old Norse hjalpa, from Proto-Germanic *helpaną. Cognate with Swedish hjälpa, English help, German helfen.
From Old Norse hyrna f, *hyrni n (not attested in Classical Old Norse, but in Middle Norwegian), from Proto-Germanic *hurnijǭ f, *hurniją n.

parole.significato: team (group of persons working or playing together)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hald (“grip, power, hold”). Also see holde (“to hold”), to which it is ultimately related.
From Old Danish haldæ, from Old Norse halda, from Proto-Germanic *haldaną, cognate with Swedish hålla, English hold, German halten, Dutch houden.
From Old Danish haldæn, from Old Norse haldinn, = the past participle of halda (“to hold”). Compare German gehalten.
From Old Norse holmr, from Proto-Germanic *hulmaz.
From Old Norse hólmganga.

parole.significato: wood, forest (of any size); (or strictly) coppice
parole.testo: From Old Danish holt, from Old Norse holt (“wood”), from Proto-Germanic *hultą (“wood”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to beat, break”). Cognate with English holt and German Holz.
From Old Danish hunung, hunigh, from Old Norse hunang, from Proto-Germanic *hunangą.
From Old Norse hopp (“jump”), from the verb hoppa, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną.
From Old Norse hoppa, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną, cognate with Swedish hoppa, English hop, German hüpfen, Dutch hoppen.
From Old Danish hor, from Old Norse hór.

parole.significato: a prostitute (a woman who earns a living by selling herself)
parole.testo: From Old Danish horæ, from Old Norse hóra, from Proto-Germanic *hōrǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“dear, loved”).
From Old Norse horn, from Proto-Norse ᚺᛟᚱᚾᚨ (horna), from Proto-Germanic *hurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂-.
From Old Danish hors, Old Norse hross n, from Proto-Germanic *hrussą, cognate with English horse, German Ross n.
From Old Norse hósti (“a cough”), hósta (“to cough”), from Proto-Germanic, from Proto-Indo-European *kwas- (“to cough”).
From Old Danish hof, from Old Norse hófr, from Proto-Germanic *hōfaz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish hov, English hoof, German Huf.

parole.significato: temple (with reference to pre-Christian Norse religion)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hof (“shrine; court”), from Proto-Germanic *hufą, cognate with German Hof (“yard, court, farmyard”), Dutch hof (“yard, court, garden”). Doublet of hof (“court”).
From Old Norse hó, compare English ho, German ho.

parole.significato: head (the body part with the brain and main sense organs)
parole.testo: From Old Danish howæth, huwæth, from Old Norse hǫfuð, haufuð, from Proto-Germanic *hafudą or *habudą, northern form of *haubudą, cf. English head, dialectal German Haupt, Dutch hoofd. The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *káput, cognate with Latin caput (“head”).
From Old Norse hǫfuðstaðr, equivalent to hoved- (“main”) + stad (“city”). In the modern language influenced by German Hauptstadt.
From Old Norse hafinn.
From Old Norse hugr, from Proto-Germanic *hugiz.

parole.significato: skin (outer covering of living tissue of a person)
parole.testo: From Old Norse húð, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish hud, English hide, German Haut, Dutch huid.
From Old Danish huvæ, from Old Norse húfa, from Proto-Germanic *hūbǭ.
From Old Norse huga (“think”).
From Old Norse hǫgg, verbal noun to hǫggva (“to hew”) (Danish hugge).

parole.significato: to cut, to hack, to slash, to hew
parole.testo: From Old Danish huggæ, hoggæ, from Old Norse hǫggva, from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną (“to hew, forge”), cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk hogga, Swedish hugga, English hew, German hauen.

parole.significato: a viper, an adder, common European adder, Vipera berus
parole.testo: From Old Danish hugorm, from Old Norse hǫggormr (“a serpent”). Equivalent to hugge + orm. Cognates include Icelandic höggormur, Faroese høggormur, Swedish huggorm and Norwegian hoggorm.

From Old Norse hol (“hole”), from Proto-Germanic *hulą, cf. English hole and German Höhle. The noun is derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *hulaz (“hollow”) (see below). Related to hule (“cave”).
From Old Norse holr (“hollow”), from Proto-Germanic *hulaz (“hollow”).

parole.significato: flesh (as a result of a certain state of nutrition)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hold (“flesh”), from Proto-Germanic *huldą.
From Old Norse hollr, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz. Cognates include Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌻𐌸𐍃 (hulþs, “clement”) and Old High German hold ( > German hold). More at hold.
Derived from Old Danish hulæ, from Old Norse hola (“cave”), from holr (“hollow”).
Derived from Old Norse hola (“to hollow”), from holr (“hollow”).
From Old Norse humarr.
From Old Norse hón (“she”), from Proto-Norse *ᚺᚨᚾᚢ (*hanu), the feminine form, with u-umlaut, of *ᚺᚨᚾᚨᛉ (*hanaʀ) (= Danish han (“he”), Old Norse hann).
From Old Norse hundr, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwn̥tós, from *ḱwṓ (“dog”).
From Old Norse hundrað (“hundred”), from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (< Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”).
From Old Norse hundrað (“hundred”).
From Old Norse hungr.
From Old Danish hus, from Old Norse hús, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą (“house”). Doublet of house.
From Old Danish husbondæ, from Old Norse húsbóndi (“master of the house”).
From Old Danish husæ, from Old Norse húsa, hýsa.
Compound of hus + frue, from Old Danish husfrugh, from Old Norse húsfrú, from Middle Low German husvruwe.
Compound of hus + herre, from Old Danish hushærre, from Old Norse húsherra.
From Old Norse húskarl.
From Old Norse hugsa, derived from the noun Old Norse hugr (“thought”) (= Danish hu).
From Old Norse húsmaðr.
From Old Danish husfrugh, hustru, from Old Norse hústrú, from húsfrú (“housewife”).
From Old Norse hvat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷód, *kʷod.
From Old Danish hwal, from Old Norse hvalr, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”).
From Old Norse hvelpr, from Proto-Germanic *hwelpaz.
From Old Norse hrosshvalr and Dutch walrus.

parole.significato: sharp (able to cut easily; able to pierce easily; offensive, critical, or acrimonious)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hwas, from Old Norse hvass, from Proto-Germanic *hwassaz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk kvass, Swedish vass, Old English hwæs and Gothic 𐍈𐌰𐍃𐍃𐌰𐌱𐌰 (ƕassaba, adverb).
From Old Danish hwætæ, from Old Norse hveiti, from Proto-Germanic *hwaitijaz.
From Old Danish hwæthæn, from Old Norse hvaðan

From Old Norse hverr (“who, each”), from Proto-Germanic *hwarjaz (“which”), *hwarjazuh (“each”), cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk kven (“who”), kvar (“each”), Swedish vars (“whose”), varje (“each”) Gothic 𐍈𐌰𐍂𐌾𐌹𐍃 (ƕarjis, “which”), 𐍈𐌰𐍂𐌾𐌹𐌶𐌿𐌷 (ƕarjizuh, “each”).

Compound of hver (“every”) + dag (“day”), from Old Norse hverr (“every”) dagr (“day”). Semantic shift of uncertain origin. Probably, from the original meaning "every day which is not a holy day". Plausibly under the influence of similar-sounding German "Werktag". Cognate with Swedish vardag and Norw
From Old Norse hvarf. verbal noun of hverve, meaning influenced by Middle Low German werf.
From Old Danish hwi, from Old Norse hví, from Proto-Germanic *hwī, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk kvi (archaic), Swedish vi (archaic), English why.
From Old Danish hwit, from Old Norse hvítr, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, cognate with English white and German weiß.
From Old Danish hwilæ, from Old Norse hvíla. Related to English while.

From Old Danish huilk, huilkin, Old Norse hvílíkr, from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz (“what kind of, what sort of”), cognate with English which, German welcher, Gothic 𐍈𐌹𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (ƕileiks). A compound of *hwaz (“who”) + *-līkaz (“shaped”).
From Old Norse hvína, from Proto-Germanic *hwīnaną. Cognate with English whine.
From Old Norse hvirfill. Cognate with German Wirbel
hvirvel + vind, from Old Norse hvirfilvindr
From Old Norse hvess, genitive singular of hvo / hvem (“who”), from Proto-Germanic *hwaz (“who”).

From Old Norse hvískra, from Proto-Germanic *hwīskrōną, a variant of *hwistlōną (in Danish hvisle, Old Norse hvísla, English whistle), *hwisprōną (in English whisper, German wispern), and *hwisplōną (in German wispeln).
From Old Danish hwar(æ), huræ, huro, from Old Norse hvar (“where”), from Proto-Germanic *hwar

From Old Danish hwænnær, hwannær, from Old Norse hvénær, a compound of 1. Old Norse hvé (“how”), from Proto-Germanic *hwē, and 2. Old Norse nær (“closer”). An alternative explanation is that is related to (or borrowed from) Middle Low German wannēr (“when”) (cf. Dutch wanneer), which is a compound o

parole.significato: to arch (to shape, build or form something so that it forms an arch)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hwælvæ, from Old Norse hvelfa, from Proto-Germanic *hwalbijaną. Cognate of Icelandic hvelfa, Norwegian kvelva, Swedish välva, Middle High German welben, German wölben, Old Saxon bihwelvian, Gothic 𐍈𐌹𐌻𐍆𐍄𐍂𐌾𐍉𐌼 (ƕilftrjōm), English whelm, Dutch welven.
From Old Norse hvæsa (“to hiss”).
From Old Danish hwæssæ, from Old Norse hvessa, from Proto-Germanic *hwassijaną, cognate with Norwegian kvesse, Swedish vässa. Derived from the adjective *hwassaz (“sharp”) (Danish hvas).

From Old Danish hyggiæ (“to think”), from Old Norse hyggja (“to think”), from Proto-Germanic *hugjaną (“to think, reconsider”). The modern meaning has been taken over from Norwegian in the 19th century.
From Old Norse hylla, from Proto-Germanic *hulþijaną, cognate with Swedish hylla. Derived from *hulþaz (“gracious”) (Danish huld).
From Old Norse hylja, from Proto-Germanic *huljaną, cognate with Swedish hölja, German hüllen, Dutch hullen.
From Old Danish høuændæ, from Old Norse hœgindi (“comfort, pillow”), from hœgr (“comfortable”).
From Old Norse hirðir, from Proto-Germanic *hirdijaz (“herdsman”), derived from Proto-Germanic *herdō (“herd”) (Danish hjord).

parole.significato: hope (belief that something hoped for can happen)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hoop, from late Old Norse hop, from Middle Low German hope.
From Old Danish haand, from Old Norse hǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *handuz.
From Old Norse hár, from Proto-Germanic *hērą, cognate with English hair, German Haar, Dutch haar.
From Old Danish harth, from Old Norse harðr (“hard”), from Proto-Germanic *harduz (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *kert-, *kret- (“strong; powerful”).
Compound of hår + fager, from Old Norse hárfagr.
From Old Danish hæthær, from Old Norse heiðr (“honor, worth”), from Proto-Germanic *haiduz.
From hæder + -lig (“honour”), from Old Danish hæthærlek, from Old Norse heiðrligr
From Old Danish hæthræ, from Old Norse heiðra.
* (imprisonment):, from Norwegian hefte. * (handle, hilt):, from Old Norse hepti. * (booklet):, from German Heft (“booklet”), from heften (“to fasten”).
From Old Norse hepta.
From Old Norse hæll (“heel”), from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz, cognate with English heel and Dutch hiel.
From Old Norse hella.

parole.significato: to happen (with or without an indirect object)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hændæ, from Old Norse henda, from Proto-Germanic *handijaną (“to seize”), cognate with Swedish hända. Derived from the noun *handuz (“hand”).

A merger of two related verbs: 1. Old Norse hengja (“to hang (transitive)”), from Proto-Germanic *hangijaną, cognate with German hängen; and 2. Old Norse hanga (“to hang (intransitive)”), from Proto-Germanic *hanhaną, cognate with English hang and German hangen. In the past tense, Danish still disti

parole.significato: That branch of the armed forces concerned mainly with ground (rather than air or naval) operations; the army.
parole.testo: From Old Norse herr, from Proto-Germanic *harjaz (“army”), from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“war”).
From Old Danish hærthæ, from Old Norse herðr, from Proto-Germanic *hardijaną.
From Old Danish hærthæ, from Old Norse herðr, from Proto-Germanic *hardį̄.
From Old Danish hæriæ, from Old Norse herja, from Proto-Germanic *harjōną, cognate with Swedish härja, English harry, German verheeren. Derived from the noun *harjaz (“army”), see hær.
hær + værk, from Old Danish hærwærk, from Old Norse hervirki. Compare Norwegian hærverk, Faroese herverk, Icelandic hervirki, herverk.
From Old Danish he(e)s, from Old Norse háss, from Proto-Germanic *haisaz.
From Old Norse hetta, from Proto-Germanic *hattijǭ. Related to hat.
From Old Danish hæfth, from Old Norse hefð, past participle of hafa (“to have”) (whence Danish have); cognate with Norwegian hevd, Swedish hävd.
From Old Danish hæfthæ, from Old Norse hefða, cognate with Norwegian hevde, Swedish hävda.

parole.significato: to raise, to elevate, to lift
parole.testo: From Old Norse hefja, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyé-, from the root *kap- (“to seize”). Compare Swedish häva, Norwegian Nynorsk hevja, English heave, West Frisian heffe, Dutch heffen, German heben.
From Old Danish hæfnd, from Old Norse hefnd (“revenge”), from hefna (“avenge”).
From Old Danish hæfnæ, from Old Norse hefna.
From Old Norse hey (“hay”).
From Old Danish høde, from Old Norse hœta, from Proto-Germanic *hwōtijaną, cognate with Swedish höta (obsolete) (now replaced by hota), Gothic 𐍈𐍉𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ƕōtjan).
From Old Danish høk, from Old Norse haukr (“hawk”), from Proto-Germanic *habukaz, cognate with Norwegian hauk, Swedish hök, English hawk, German Habicht, Dutch havik.

From Old Danish høgh, from Old Norse (east) *haugʀ, (west) hár, hór, from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz, *haugaz (“high”), cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk høg, Norwegian Bokmål høy, Swedish hög, English high, German hoch, Dutch hoog.
From Old Danish høgh, from Old Norse haugr, from Proto-Germanic *haugaz (“height, high place, hill”), cognate with Norwegian haug, Swedish hög, Old High German houc.

Equivalent to høj (“high”) + -de (noun suffix): from Old Danish høgdh, from Old Norse hæð, from Proto-Germanic *hauhiþō. Other cognates are Swedish höjd, English height and Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐌷𐌹𐌸𐌰 (hauhiþa). In Danish and Swedish, the noun has been remodelled after the adjective.
From Old Danish høghræ, from Old Norse hǿgri, a comparative of the adjective hǿgr (“convenient”).

parole.significato: a depression in a river or stream or a cavern
parole.testo: From Old Danish hyl n, from Old Norse hylr m, from Proto-Germanic *hulwiją, cognate with Norwegian høl m, Old High German huliwa (“puddle”), German Hüle, Hülbe (“village pond”, dialect).
From Old Norse hǿna, from Proto-Germanic *hōnijǭ, related to *hanjō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kan- (“to sing”), *kana-.
From Old Norse hǫrr.

parole.significato: to hear (to perceive with the ears)
parole.testo: From Old Danish høræ, from Old Norse heyra, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną, cognate with Swedish höra, English hear, German hören. The verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti, which is also the source of Ancient Greek ἀκούω (akoúō).
From Old Norse heysláttr.

From Old Danish høst, from Old Norse haust n, haustr m, from Proto-Germanic *harbistaz, *harbustaz, cognate with Swedish höst (“autumn”), English harvest, German Herbst (“autumn”), Dutch herfst (“autumn”) and Latin carpere.
From høst (“harvest”) + -e, from Old Norse hausta.
From Old Norse heytjúga, heytýja.
From Old Norse hǫfðingi.
From the Old Norse prepositional phrase í fjǫrð. See fjor for more.
From Old Norse í gær, í gjár (“yesterday”) (whence Icelandic í gær and Faroese í gjár).

parole.significato: tomorrow (on the day after the present day)
parole.testo: From Old Norse í morgin, á morgin.
From Old Norse í, from Proto-Germanic *in, from Proto-Indo-European *en.
From Old Danish æ, e, from Old Norse æ, ei, ey, from Proto-Germanic *aiwi (“forever”), *aiwaz. May always be used as a prefix.
From Old Norse ið.
From Old Norse í gegn (“against”).

parole.significato: leech (a blood-sucking animal of the subclass Hirudinea)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ígull (“sea urchin”), from Proto-Germanic *igilaz (“hedgehog”), cognate with Swedish igle (“leech”), German Igel (“hedgehog”), Dutch egel (“hedgehog”). The sense is influenced by Middle Low German egel, ile (“leech”), which derives a related noun, *egulaz, which is also the source of
Old Danish igiald, from Old Norse iðgjǫld (“payback”).
From Old Danish ikkæ, ækki, from Old Norse ekki (“not”), cognate with Jutish itt, Swedish icke, inte. The neuter of the Old Norse pronoun engi (“nobody, no”), see ingen.

parole.significato: fire (flames from an object that burns)
parole.testo: From Old Danish eld, from Old Norse eldr (“fire”), from Proto-Germanic *ailidaz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk eld, Swedish eld, Old Saxon ēld, Old English ǣled.
From Old Danish illæ. Originally the adverb of the obsolete adjective ild, from Old Norse íllr (adverb illa), from Proto-Germanic *ilhilaz, cognate with Swedish illa (only an adverb).
From Old Norse (í) millum. Compare Faroese ímillum, Swedish emellan.

parole.significato: in (indicating movement from exterior to interior)
parole.testo: From Old Danish in, from Old Norse inn.
From Old Danish innænbyrthæs, from Old Norse innbyrðis (“within the railing of a ship”). Cognate with Swedish inbördes.
From Old Danish innæn, innan, from Old Norse innan, from Proto-Norse ᛁᚾᚨᚾᚨ (inana), from Proto-Germanic *innanē.
From Old Norse innanlands, a compound of innan (“within”) + land (“land”). Compare Norwegian Bokmål innenlands, innalands and Swedish inomlands.
From Old Norse innfœddr, influenced by German eingeboren. Compare Old Norse innborinn.
From Old Norse innri, from Proto-Germanic *innarô, cognate with Norwegian indre, Swedish inre, German innerer, English inner. Utilamtely derived from the adverb *in (“in”).
From Old Norse engi, enginn, from einn (“one”) + -gi (“not”).
From Old Norse Írar m pl (“Irishmen”), borrowed from Old Irish Ériu (“Ireland”), perhaps from Proto-Celtic *Φīweryū (hence Latin Hibernia), from Proto-Indo-European *piH-wer- (“fat”).
From Old Norse írskr (“Irish”), from Old Norse Írar m pl (“Irishmen”), see irer.
From Old Danish is, iis, from Old Norse íss, from Proto-Germanic *īsą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyH-.

parole.significato: to cool with ice; to cover with ice
parole.testo: is + -e, from Old Norse ísa. Compare Swedish isa, Norwegian ise, Middle Low German isen and German eisen.
From Old Norse íslendingr, from Ísland (“Iceland”).
From Old Danish issæ, from Old Norse hjarsi (“crown of the head”), from Proto-Germanic *hersô.

parole.significato: lard, grease; a solid but soft fat from the intestines of certain animals
parole.testo: From Old Danish istær, from Old Norse ístr, from Proto-Germanic *instraz (“intestine”).

From i (“in”) and Old Danish sær (“separately, independently”), from Old Norse sér dative of third-person reflexive pronoun Old Norse sik. Cognate with Swedish isär, Norwegian Nynorsk især, Norwegian Bokmål især.
From Old Norse í tvau (“in two (parts)”), originally a prepositional phrase.
From Old Norse já (“yes”).

parole.significato: jarl (a title given to the highest noblemen in Norse times.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse jarl, from Proto-Norse ᛖᚱᛁᛚᚨᛉ (erilaʀ), from Proto-Germanic *erlaz, akin to Old English eorl (English earl).
From Old Danish iak, iæk, iægh, æk, ak, from Old Norse ek, Old East Norse iak, from Proto-Germanic *ek, *ik (“I”), from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm, *eǵh₂óm.

parole.significato: second person plural objective case – you, yourselves
parole.testo: Archaic eder, from Old Danish idher, edher, Old Norse yðr, from Proto-Germanic *izwiz, dative/accusative of *jūz (“you (all)”) (see I). Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål dere, Swedish er, English you and German euch.

From Old Norse yðvarr, from Proto-Germanic *izweraz, possessive of *jūz (“you (all)”) (see I). Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål deres, Swedish er, English your and German euer. In most Germanic languages, it is an inflected adjective, but in modern Danish (and Norwegian), it is uninflected. In archaizing

parole.significato: iron (metallic chemical element having atomic number 26, and symbol Fe)
parole.testo: From Old Danish jarn, from Old Norse járn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarną, cognate with English iron and German Eisen. The Germanic word is an old loan from Proto-Celtic *īsarnom, cf. Irish iarann.

parole.significato: yes (used to contradict a negative statement or negatively phrased question)
parole.testo: From Old Norse jaur, compare Swedish jo.
From Old Danish iorþ, iorth, from Old Norse jǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *erþō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁er-.

From Old Norse jǫrðber, from Proto-Germanic *erþōbazją; equivalent to jord (“earth, soil, ground”) + bær (“berry”), as the berries are close to the ground, cognate with Icelandic jarðarber, Old Swedish iordhbær, Old English eorþberġe, Dutch aardbei, and German Erdbeere.

parole.significato: to put down, to flatten, to floor
parole.testo: From Old Danish iordhæ, from Old Norse jarða.
From Old Norse jarðeskr, equivalent to jord + -isk.
jord + -s- + mon. from Old Norse jarðmunr, last part of the word is from Old Norse munr (“value, difference”).
From Old Norse jól, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *jehwlą, *jeulō.
From Old Norse jótar m pl, from Proto-Germanic *eutaz, cognate with Old English Ēotas, Īotas.
Equivalent to jyde (“Jute, person from Jutland”) + -sk. From Old Danish iuzk, Old Norse józkr.

From Old Danish iæthtæ, arisen by rebracketing from iætæn (with the ending -n interpreted as a suffixed definite article), from Old Norse jǫtunn, from Proto-Germanic *etunaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-.

From Old Danish iafn, iæfn, from Old Norse jafn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz (“even, level”), cognate with Swedish jämn, Norwegian Bokmål jevn, Norwegian Bokmål/Norwegian Nynorsk jamn, English even, Dutch even, effen, German eben.

parole.significato: to make (something) flat, even and smooth, to level out
parole.testo: From Old Danish iæfnæ, from Old Norse jafna.
From late Old Norse kabill, from Middle Low German kabel, from Latin capulum.
From Old Danish kakæ, from Old Norse kaka, from Proto-Germanic *kakǭ.

parole.significato: vocation, calling; an inclination to undertake a certain kind of work, especially a religious career
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse kall.
From Old Norse kalla (“call”), itself from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną (“call, shout”).

parole.significato: calf (a young cow or bull, also used of some other large animals, e.g., the offspring of a deer, whale, elephant, or rh…
parole.testo: From Old Norse kalfr (“calf”), from Proto-Germanic *kalbaz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish kalv, Dutch kalf, German Kalb, and English calf.

From Old Norse kambr, from Proto-Germanic *kambaz, Norwegian, Swedish kam, English comb, German Kamm. The Germanic noun goes back to Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth, peg”), which is also the source of Sanskrit: जम्भः (jámbhaḥ, “tooth”), Ancient Greek γόμφος (gómphos, “peg”), Polish ząb (“tooth”
From late Old Norse kamell, from Latin camelus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos, “camel”).

parole.significato: jug (large serving vessel, amount a jug can hold)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kanna.
From Old Norse ker.

parole.significato: farmhand (a man working at a farm)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse karl (“man”), from Proto-Norse *ᚲᚨᚱᛁᛚᚨᛉ (*karilaʀ), from Proto-Germanic *karilaz, cognate with English churl, German Kerl, Dutch kerel.
From Old Norse karmr, compare Icelandic: karmur.

parole.significato: karve; a multipurpose intermediate size Viking longship
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse karfi.
From Old Norse kast, verbal noun to kasta (“throw”).
From Old Danish kastæ, from Old Norse kasta, from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), cognate with Norwegian kaste and Swedish kasta. English cast is borrowed from Old Norse.
Inherited from Old Norse kǫttr, from Proto-Germanic *kattuz.
From Old Norse ketill.
From Old Danish kænnæ, from Old Norse kenna (“know, feel”), from Proto-Germanic *kannijaną. Cognate with Swedish känna, German kennen, English ken. A causative form of *kunnaną (“to know”).
From Old Norse kenni. Compare Swedish känn.
From genkende + -lig. From Old Danish kænnælik (“sensitive”), from Old Norse kenniligr.
From Old Norse kennari, from kenna.
Borrowed from Old Norse kenning, from the verb kenna (“to know”).
From Old Danish kiærnæ, kiarnæ, from Old Norse kjarni (“core”), from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“core, kernel”). Cognate with Swedish kärna and German Kern.

parole.significato: candle (light source consisting of a wick embedded in a solid, flammable substance such as wax, tallow, or paraffin)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kerti, from Middle Low German kerte.

From Old Danish kith, from Old Norse kið (“young goat”), from Proto-Germanic *kidją, *kittīną (“goatling, kid”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gʰaydn-, *ǵʰaydn- (“goat”) or Proto-Indo-European *gidʰ- (“kid, goatling, little goat”). Compare Swedish and Norwegian Bokmål kid, English kid, German Ki

parole.significato: spring, fountain, source (a place where water emerges from the ground)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kelda, from Proto-Germanic *kaldijǭ, cognate with Norwegian kjelde, Swedish källa. Derived from *kaldaz (“cold”).
From Old Norse kitla, from Proto-Germanic *kitilōną, cognate with Swedish kittla, English kittle, German kitzeln.
From Old Norse ketlingr, diminutive form of ketta (“cat”). Cognate with Swedish källing.
From Old Norse kinn, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénu- (“cheek”). Compare Swedish kind, Norwegian and Icelandic kinn, Low German and German Kinn, Dutch kin, English chin.
From Old Norse kippa (“basket”), from Proto-Germanic *kippǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gey- (“to bend, twist, entwine”). Influenced by Middle Low German kiffe (“hut”).

parole.significato: to tilt or swing (about a horizontal axis)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kippa (“to snatch”), from Middle Low German kippen. Compare German kippen and Icelandic kippa.

From Old Danish kirk(i)æ, kyrk(i)æ, from Old Norse kirkja, from Old English ċiriċe (“church”), from Byzantine Greek κυριακόν (kuriakón, “church”), a neuter form of κυριακός (kuriakós, “belonging to the lord”), from κύριος (kúrios, “ruler, lord”).
Old Norse kirkjugarðr, equivalently kirke (“church”) + gård (“yard”).
From Old Norse kista, from Latin cista, from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē, “box”).
From Old Danish kiurtæl, from Old Norse kyrtill, from Old English cyrtel.
From Old Norse klappa, from Proto-Germanic *klappōną.
From Old Danish klærk, from Old Norse klerkr, from Old English clerc, from Late Latin clēricus, from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós).
From Old Danish klinæ, from Old Norse klína, from Proto-Germanic *kleinijan-, from Proto-Indo-European *gley-.
From Old Norse klippa (“to clip”).

From Old Norse klettr (“crag”). Cognate with Norwegian klett (“cliff, summit”), Scots clett (“rock in the sea, separated from the cliffs on the mainland”), Old English clit, Ancient Greek κλιτύς f (klitús, “hill”). Doublet of klint.
From Old Norse kló, from Proto-Germanic *klawō

From Old Norse klokka, from Middle Low German klocke, from Medieval Latin clocca, probably of Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos (“bell”) (compare Welsh cloch, Irish clog), from Proto-Indo-European *klēg-, *klōg- (onomatopoeia).

parole.significato: hoof (of a pig or cow etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Danish kløf, from Old Norse klauf.
From Old Norse klútr, itself borrowed from Old English clut (“patch”).
From Old Danish klæthæ, from Old Norse klæði, borrowed from Old Frisian klāth, klēth or Old English clāþ, clǣþ, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą (“garment”). Cognate with English cloth and German Kleid.
From Old Norse klæða, borrowed from Old English *clāþian, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþijaną, *klaiþōną (“to clothe”). Cognate with English clothe and German kleiden.
From Old Norse kleyja.
A conversion of klaa(d)e, from Old Danish klathæ, from Old Norse kláði, from Proto-Germanic *klawiþô.
From Old Norse kljúfa, from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną (“to cleave, split”), from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ-.

parole.significato: page (noble youth serving an adult noble)
parole.testo: Old Norse knapi, compare Icelandic knapi and German Knabe
From Old Norse knappr, from Proto-Germanic *knappô.
Borrowed from Old Norse knǫrr.
From Old Norse kneppa (“squeeze”). Compare Swedish knäppa (“snap”).
From Old Danish knif, from Old Norse knífr (“knife”), from Proto-Germanic *knībaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gneybʰ-.
From Old Norse knúi, from Proto-Germanic *knūwan. Compare Swedish knoge; further Danish knoge, German Knochen, Dutch knook, knokkel, English knuckle. Related to knogle and knuge.
From Old Danish knutæ, from Old Norse knútr.

parole.significato: to squeeze, clutch, clench, embrace, hug, clasp
parole.testo: From Old Norse knoka.
From Old Norse knosa (“to beat, bruise”). Cognate with Old High German zerchnusen.
From Old Norse knýta, from Proto-Germanic *knuttijaną.

parole.significato: piece of cloth tied together crosswise at the corners, (used to carry clothes or small items)
parole.testo: From Old Norse knýti. Related to knude. Cognate with Swedish knyte
From Old Norse kné, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu (“knee”).
From Old Norse *kōʀ (east), kýr (west), from Proto-Germanic *kōz.

From Old Danish koddæ, from Old Norse koddi (“pillow”), from Proto-Germanic *kuddô (“bag, sag, purse”), from Proto-Indo-European *gewt- (“pouch, sack”), from *gew- (“to bend, bow, arch, vault, curve”). Cognates include Swedish kudde and English cod

parole.significato: cock (male gallinaceous bird; dialectal, except when speaking about pheasants)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kokr, from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz.
Last part of the word is from Old Norse kǫs (literally “heap, pile”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kas- From Proto-Germanic *kasō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ǵ-es- (“to throw”)
From Old Danish kald, from Old Norse kaldr, from Proto-Germanic *kaldaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).
From Old Norse kolfr. Mixed with kolbe.

From Old Danish komæ, kommæ, kombæ, from Old Norse koma, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną, cognate with English come, German kommen. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (“to step”), cf. Latin veniō, Ancient Greek βαίνω (baínō) (whence also base and basis).
From Old Danish kona, konæ, kunæ, from Old Norse kona, from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn.

Older konning, from Old Danish kunung, from Old Norse konungr (“king”), from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz (“king”), cognate with Swedish konung, English king, German König, Dutch koning. Derived from *kunją (“kin, clan”) (Danish køn).
From Old Norse konungdómr, from Proto-Germanic *kuningadōmaz. Equivalent to konge + -dømme.

parole.significato: A nation having as supreme ruler, a kingdom.
parole.testo: From Old Norse konungríki, from Proto-Germanic *kuningarīkiją. Equivalent to konge (“king”) + rige (“realm”). Compare Norwegian kongerike, Swedish kungarike, Dutch koninkrijk, German Königreich.

parole.significato: A cup; A concave vessel for holding liquid, generally adorned with either a handle or a stem (confer goblet, glass.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse koppr, from Middle Low German kop, from Latin cuppa.
From Old Norse kórr, from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós).

From Old Norse korn, from Proto-Germanic *kurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Related to kerne (“kernel, core”), from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“kernel, core”). Possibly also related to kærne (“(butter) churn”), from Proto-Germanic *kirnijǭ (“churn”) (see that entry for more).

parole.significato: food (any substance consumed by living organisms to sustain life)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kostr, from Middle Low German kost, koste, German Kosten, borrowed from Medieval Latin costa, which is derived from the verb constare.

parole.significato: to cost; to have a price; to be for sale
parole.testo: From Old Norse kosta, from Middle Low German kosten, from Latin cōnstāre.
From Old Norse krabbi, from Old English crabba.

parole.significato: to move awkwardly; to stumble, lumber
parole.testo: From Old Norse krabba. Related to Dutch krabben and Ancient Greek γράφειν (gráphein).
From Old Norse kraptr, krǫptr, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz, cognate with English craft, German Kraft, Dutch kracht and West Frisian krêft.

parole.significato: crow, especially carrion crow and hooded crow (Corvus corone) and (Corvus cornix)
parole.testo: From Old Danish krakæ, from Old Norse kráka (“crow”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”). Onomatopoeic.
From Old Norse krama (“to press, squeeze”), from kremja (“to crush”).
From Old Norse kram, from Middle Low German kräm (“fine cloth; also used for merchant tents, thus later a synonym for merchandise”), probably ultimately of Slavic origin; see German Kram.
From Old Norse kremja.

From late Old Norse kranz, from Middle Low German kranz, from Middle High German kranz, from Old High German kranz, probably altered from krenz, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *kringaz (“circle, ring”).
From Old Norse krǫf f, from Proto-Germanic *krafō, related to Proto-Germanic *krafjaną (“to demand”) (see kræve).
From late Old Norse kragi, from Middle Low German krage, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷer- (“to devour”).
From Old Norse krafla.
Old Norse kringla
From Old Norse kristinn (cf. runic ᚴᚱᛁᛋᛏᚾᚬ (kristną), acc.pl). Borrowed via Old English cristen or Middle Low German kristen from Latin Chrīstiānus, derived from Chrīstus + -iānus.
From Old Danish krok, from Old Norse krókr (“hook”), from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz.
From Old Norse kroppr, from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz. Cognate with Swedish kropp, English crop and German Kropf.

From late Old Norse krús, maybe from Middle Low German krūs, krōs, of uncertain ultimate origin, but Pokorny proposes an ultimate derivation from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, bend”), similar to Proto-Germanic *krōkaz (“something bent, crooked”), *krukjō (“staff”).
Verbal noun to krybe (“crawl, creep”), from Old Norse krjúpa.

parole.significato: to crawl, creep (to move slowly or carefully)
parole.testo: From Old Danish krypæ, from Old Norse krjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *kreupaną. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål krype, Swedish krypa, English creep, Dutch kruipen.
From Old Norse krás, Proto-Germanic *krēsō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gras-, see also Ancient Greek γράω (gráō, “to eat, gnaw”). The Danish form is influenced by the verb, see kræse.

parole.significato: to serve something delicious, to give a treat
parole.testo: From Old Danish kræsæ, from Old Norse kræsask, from Proto-Germanic *krēsijaną, derived from the noun *krēsō (= Old Norse krás, Danish kræs). See kræs (“something delicious”), which shares the same root.
From Old Danish krævæ, kræviæ, from Old Norse krefja, from Proto-Germanic *krafjaną (“to demand”), cognate with Swedish kräva, English crave.
From Old Norse kúga (“to cow, force”).
From Old Norse kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą, cognate with Swedish kol, German Kohle, Dutch kool, English coal.
From Old Norse kuldi.
From Old Norse kúla (“swelling”), from Proto-Germanic *kūlǭ, cognate with Swedish kula (“bump”), German Kaule (dated), Kuhle (“hollow”, from Low German), Dutch kuil (“pit”).
Older ikkun, a contraction of Old Danish ække uten (“nothing but”), from Old Norse ekki (“not”) and útan (“without, except”).
From Old Danish kunnær, kundær, from Old Norse kunnr, from Proto-Germanic *kunþaz. Cognate with English couth.

parole.significato: to be able, can (with an infinitive)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kunna, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, cognate with English con, German können. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”), which is also the source of the Danish words kende (“to know”), kunde (“customer”), kundskab (“knowledge”), kunst (“art”).
From Old Danish kwal, from Old Norse kvǫl, from Proto-Germanic *kwalō. Cognate of German Qual, Dutch kwaal, Old English cwalu. Compare origin of kvæle.
From Old Norse kvíga.

parole.significato: to equivocate, hesitate; to be reluctant
parole.testo: From Old Danish kvithæ, from Old Norse kvíða. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kvida/kvi, Icelandic kvíða and Swedish kvida.
From Old Norse kvik(k)r or borrowed from Middle Low German quik, from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz (“alive”). Doublet of kæk and kvæg.

From Old Danish quinnæ, kvinnæ, from Old Norse kvenna, the genitive plural indefinite of kona (“woman, wife”), from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn (“woman”). Related to English queen via Proto-Germanic *kwēniz.
From Old Norse kvennkyn.
From Old Norse kvistr.
From Old Norse kvittr, from Middle Low German quit, from Medieval Latin quitus, quittus, from Latin quiētus (“quiet, calm”).
From Old Norse kveða, from Proto-Germanic *kweþaną (“to say”), cognate with English quoth (“said”), Gothic 𐌵𐌹𐌸𐌰𐌽 (qiþan, “to say”).

From Old Danish quik, qwegh (“alive, lively”), from Old Norse kvikr, from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz, cognate with English quick, German quick (from Low German), keck. Doublet of kvik, kæk, and kvaj. The modern use as a noun is an abbreviation of Old Danish qwikfæ, Old Norse kvikfé.
From Old Danish kwæld, from Old Norse kveld, from Proto-Germanic *kweldą, *kwildiz
From Old Danish kwæliæ, kwælæ, from Old Norse kvelja (“to torment, torture”), from Proto-Germanic *kwaljaną. Cognate with Swedish kvälja, English quell and German quälen (“to torture”).
From Old Norse kvirr, kyrr, from Proto-Germanic *kwerruz, cognate with Swedish kvar, German kirre, Gothic 𐌵𐌰𐌹𐍂𐍂𐌿𐍃 (qairrus).

parole.significato: a grinder, mill (mechanical or electrical machine that pulverizes or grinds a material into powder)
parole.testo: From Old Danish kwærn, quærn, from Old Norse kvern, from Proto-Germanic *kwernō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerewn- (“millstone”). Compare Old English cweorn.
From Old Danish kykling, from Old Norse kjúklingr (“chicken”).
From Old Danish kyndælmæssæ, from Old Norse kyndilsmessa. Calque of Latin missa candelarum.
From Old Norse koss, from Proto-Germanic *kussaz (“a kiss”). Probably an onomatopoeia.

parole.significato: to frighten, especially in a deterring way
parole.testo: From Old Norse kjósa (“to choose, influence with magic”), from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews-.

parole.significato: to kiss (to touch with the lips)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kyssa, from Proto-Germanic *kussijaną (“to kiss”), from *kussaz (“a kiss”).
From Old Norse kápa, from Latin capa. Doublet of kappe (“cape, cloak”) (via German).

parole.significato: exuberant, happy in an energetic way
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse kátr, from Proto-Germanic *kanhtaz. Cognate with Swedish kåt.
From Old Danish kaal, from Old Norse kál.
From Old Norse *koʀ (East), kør (West), from Proto-Germanic *kuzą (“choice”). Cognate with Norwegian kår and Swedish kor. Derived from the verb *keusaną (“to choose”).
From Old Danish kiæft, from Old Norse kjaptr, from Proto-Germanic *kebutaz. Cognate with Swedish käft, Norwegian kjeft, Icelandic kjaftur, and Faroese kjaftur. Related to kæbe and kaje.
From Old Norse kellari, from Latin cellārium.

parole.significato: a small (usually single-person) sled that is unpowered and therefore only goes downhill, used as a toy
parole.testo: From Old Norse kjalki
From Old Norse kerling, from karl (“man”) (cf. the alternative form: kall). Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål kjerring, Norwegian Nynorsk kjerring, Swedish kärring, käring.
From Old Norse kelfa.

parole.significato: to comb with a comb or a fine-tooth comb
parole.testo: From Old Norse kemba, from Proto-Germanic *kambijaną.
From Old Norse keppr.
From Old Norse kjarr, from Proto-Germanic *kerzą (“brushwood”), cf. Swedish kärr.
From Old Norse kærr, likely from Old Norman ker, quer (Old French chier, cher), from Latin cārus.
From Old Norse kæra. Cognate with English care.
From Old Norse kærligr, equivalent to kær (dear) + -lig (-like).

kærlig + -hed, Roughly from Old Danish kærlek, kærlegh (“love”), from Old Norse kærleikr. The suffix "-lig" in "kærlig" was likely mixed up with another (now obsolete and unproductive) homophonous suffix (Cf. bolig, vejrlig), and therefore "-hed" was added. Cf. also Swedish kärlek.

From Old Norse kirna, from Proto-Germanic *kirnijǭ, cognate with Icelandic kirna, Swedish kärna, English churn, German Kirne, Karn (regional words). Related to Proto-Germanic *kernǭ in Icelandic kerna (“creme”), Middle Dutch kerne, German Kern (regional word) and the following verb. These words may
From Old Norse *kirna, from Proto-Germanic *kirnijaną, cognate with Icelandic kirna, Swedish kärna, English churn, German kirnen, Dutch karnen.

parole.significato: candle (light source consisting of a wick embedded in a solid, flammable substance such as wax, tallow, or paraffin)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kerti, from Middle Low German kerte.
From Old Norse kaup, compare with købe.

From Old Danish køpæ (“buy, purchase”), from Old Norse kaupa, past tense keypta, from Proto-Germanic *kaupōną, *kaupijaną, cognate with German kaufen and Dutch kopen. The Germanic verb is probably a loan from Latin caupō (“tradesman”).

From Old Danish køpslaghæ, from Old Norse kaupslaga, from Middle Low German kopslagen (“to settle a deal by shaking hands”). Derived from the noun kopslach. Cognates include Swedish köpslå and Norwegian Bokmål kjøpslå.
Equivalent to købe (“to buy”) + stad (“city”). From Old Norse kaupstaðr. Compare Norwegian kjøpstad and Swedish köpstad, Swedish köping, Dutch koopstad.
From Old Norse kjǫt, from Proto-Germanic *ketwą. Cognate with Icelandic kjöt, Faroese kjøt, Norwegian Bokmål kjøtt, Norwegian Nynorsk kjøt and Swedish kött.
From Old Norse kjǫlr (“keel”), from Proto-Germanic *keluz (“keel”), cognate with Norwegian kjøl, Swedish köl. English keel, German Kiel and Dutch kiel are all borrowed from Old Norse.
From Old Norse kœla, from Proto-Germanic *kōlijaną, cognate with German kühlen, Dutch koelen. Derived from the adjective *kōlaz (“cool”).
From Old Norse kylfa
From Old Norse kjǫlr (“keel”) + syll (“sill”).

parole.significato: sex (the biological division in male and female individuals)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kyn (“kin”), from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“kin, descent”). Cognate with Swedish kön, Norwegian Bokmål kjønn, English kin, Latin genus and Ancient Greek γένος (génos).
From Old Norse kœnn (“skilled, capable”), from Proto-Germanic *kōniz (“clever”). Cognate with English keen and German kühn (“daring”).

parole.significato: to drive (to be the driver of a vehicle or to convey somebody in a vehicle)
parole.testo: From Old Danish køræ, from Old Norse keyra, from Proto-Germanic *kaurijaną, Norwegian kjøre, Swedish köra.
From Old Danish lat, from Old Norse latr, from Proto-Germanic *lataz, from Proto-Indo-European *lē(y)d-.

parole.significato: bed (platform of a truck, trailer, railcar, or other vehicle that supports the load to be hauled), e.g. truckbed
parole.testo: From Old Norse hlað (“heap, stack”).
From Old Norse hlaða, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþǭ, derived from *hlaþaną (“to load”) (see below).
From Old Danish latæ, from Old Norse láta, from Proto-Germanic *lētaną.
From Old Norse hlaða, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną.

parole.significato: layer, coat (a coherent mass spread on the top or on the outside of something else)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lag, from Proto-Germanic *lagą. Doublet of lav (“guild”) and lov (“law”).
From Old Norse lax (“salmon”), from Proto-Germanic *lahsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *laks- (“salmon”).
From Old Norse lami, from Proto-Germanic *lamaz. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *lomiti.
From Old Danish lamb, from Old Norse lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz (“lamb”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁l̥h₁-on-bʰ-os- (“lamb”)
From Old Norse lampi, from Middle Low German lampe, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “torch”).

parole.significato: country (a geographical area that is politically independent)
parole.testo: From Old Danish land, from Old Norse land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, cognate with English land, German Land.

parole.significato: to land (get down to the ground or into the water after a flight or a jump)
parole.testo: From Old Danish lændhe, from Old Norse lenda (“to land”), Proto-Germanic *landijaną, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk lenda, Swedish landa (older lända), English land, German landen (older länden). Derived from the noun *landą (“land”). The verb has taken over the vowel from the noun in Danish.
From Old Danish landæmærkæ, from Old Norse landamerki. Cognate with Swedish landmärke, Norwegian landemerke, German Landmarke.
From Old Norse landmaðr, equivalent to land + mand. Compare landsmand.
By surface analysis, land + nam. Learned borrowing from Old Norse landnám.
From land (“land”) + -skab (“-ship”), from Old Norse landskapr.
Old Norse landsmaðr, equivalent to land (“country”) + -s- + mand (“man”). Compare landmand.

From Old Danish langer, lang, from Old Norse langr, from Proto-Germanic *langaz (“long”), cognate with Swedish lång, English long, German lang. The adjective goes back to Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos, *dl̥h₁gʰós (“long”), which is also the source of Latin longus, Ancient Greek δολιχός (dolikhós).

parole.significato: ling, common ling (the fish Molva molva, similar to the cod)
parole.testo: From Old Norse langa, from Proto-Germanic *langǭ, *langijǭ, cognate with Swedish långa, English ling, Dutch leng, German Leng. Derived from the adjective *langaz (“long”).
From Old Norse langskip.
From Old Norse lǫstr, from the root of Proto-Germanic *lahaną (“to reproach, blame”), see also Old High German lastar (“vice”).

From Old Norse hlátr, from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”). Cognate with Norwegian lått, English laughter and German Gelächter. Derived from the verb *hlahjaną (“to laugh”), cf. Danish le, English laugh, German lachen.
From Old Danish lagh, from Old Norse lágr, from Proto-Germanic *lēgaz, cognate with Norwegian låg, Swedish låg. English low is borrowed from Old Norse.
From Old Norse lag (“layer”), from Proto-Germanic *lagą. Doublet of lag, [Term?], and layer (the Old Norse plural lǫg lives on in Danish lov and English law).
From Old Norse laga, derived from lag (“layer”). Cognate with Norwegian lage, Swedish laga.
From Old Norse lé (“scythe”), from Proto-Germanic *lewô, cognate with Norwegian ljå and Swedish lie.

parole.significato: to laugh (show mirth by peculiar movement of the muscles of the face and emission of sounds)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hlæja, from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną, cognate with English laugh and German lachen.

parole.significato: joint (movable connection between the bones in a body or a minor exterior part of the body; also of joints in a plant)
parole.testo: From Old Danish lith, from Old Norse liðr, from Proto-Germanic *liþuz.

parole.significato: gate (in a fence or at a level crossing)
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse hliðr, from Proto-Germanic *hlidą, cognate with Swedish lid (“gate”), English lid, German lid (“eyelid”).
Inherited from Old Norse leiðr (“uncomfortable, tired”), Proto-Germanic *laiþaz, cognate with English loath, German leid (“distressing”), Dutch leed (“sad”).
From Old Danish lethæ, from Old Norse leiða (“to lead”), from Proto-Germanic *laidijaną (“to lead”), cognate with English lead, German leiten. It is a causative of the verb *līþaną (“to go, pass”).
From Old Danish letæ, from Old Norse leita (“to seek, search”), from Proto-Germanic *wlaitōną, cognate with Old English wlātian (“to look upon”), Gothic 𐍅𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍄𐍉𐌽 (wlaitōn, “to look around”).
From Old Danish lethæ, from Old Norse leiða, derived from the adjective Old Norse leiðr (Danish led (“disgusting”)).

parole.significato: lodestar, star (or different thing) used for navigation
parole.testo: From Old Norse leiðarstjarna (“lodestar”), from Proto-Germanic *laidō + *sternǭ, equivalent to lede + stjerne.
From Old Norse liðugr, from Proto-Germanic *liþugaz, influenced by Middle Low German ledich.
From Old Danish lething, from Old Norse leiðangr.
From Old Norse leikr, from Proto-Germanic *laikaz.
